# Where We Stand

## Recap of Units 6–11

::: {.incremental}
- **Unit 6**: local atomic environments + universal MLIPs (MACE-MP-0, M3GNet, CHGNet)
- **Unit 7**: graphs as the structural language of crystals
- **Unit 8**: regression with materials-aware splits and OOD discipline
- **Unit 9**: neural networks as scalable surrogates
- **Unit 10–11**: representation learning, latent spaces, and what an embedding actually means
- All of the above is **forward** modelling: structure $\to$ property
- Today we invert the arrow: **property target $\to$ structure**
:::

::: {.notes}
**Open with the arc, not the topic.** Six units of machinery — environments, graphs, honest regression, scalable surrogates, latent spaces — and every single one of them answers the same question: *given* a structure, what does it do? Say that sentence, pause, then flip it: nobody funds a lab to predict properties of structures we already have. The funded question is the inverse one.

**One sentence per unit, no more.** U6 gave us universal MLIPs (they return as the funnel's workhorse in Part V — flag that now). U7 gave the graph language every generator's score network speaks. U8 taught OOD discipline — generated structures are *by construction* out-of-distribution for our surrogates, so U8's warnings apply with a vengeance today. U10–11 taught what a latent space is — CDVAE literally samples from one.

**Classroom move.** Ask: "Name a materials problem where someone hands you the *property* first." Collect two or three (battery voltage window, thermoelectric zT, a magnet without rare earths). Every answer is an inverse problem. This lands the motivation better than any slide.

**Pacing.** ~3 min. Do not re-teach the old units; this is a runway, not a recap exam.
:::

## From Prediction to Inverse Design

::: {.incremental}
- A predictor tells you what a *given* structure will do
- A discovery loop wants the *opposite*: name a property target, get candidate structures
- Classical inverse design = high-throughput screening + grid search — does not scale
- Modern inverse design = **generative models** that sample structures conditioned on the target
- Output: a stream of candidate crystals, each with composition, lattice, coordinates, and (optionally) space group
- The candidate stream then enters a filtering funnel (MLIP relax $\to$ DFT $\to$ uncertainty $\to$ experiment)
:::

::: {.notes}
**Why screening does not scale — make the number concrete.** Even restricting to quaternary compositions of 60 usable elements gives $\binom{60}{4} \approx 5\times 10^5$ chemical systems before you pick stoichiometry, prototype, or cell — the structure space per system is effectively unbounded. Grid search dies of combinatorics; high-throughput DFT dies of cost (each relaxation is CPU-days). Screening also has a subtler flaw: it can only rank *enumerated* candidates, and enumeration is always prototype-substitution in disguise — you will never screen your way to a genuinely new structural motif.

**The conceptual pivot, said precisely.** A generative model does not invert $f$; it learns a *distribution* $p(x \mid y^\star)$ and lets you sample. That reframing — inverse design as conditional sampling, not root-finding — is the single most examinable sentence of the lecture.

**Pre-empt.** "Why not gradient descent on $x$ through the property predictor?" — because $x$ is discrete-plus-continuous (species + lattice + coordinates), the predictor is only trustworthy on-manifold, and naive optimisation walks straight off it into adversarial garbage. That failure is exactly what U8 called OOD abuse of a regressor.

**Plant the funnel image now.** The generator is the *widest* stage of a funnel, not the product. We spend Part V entirely inside that funnel.

**Pacing.** ~4 min. End Part 0 at ~7 min.
:::

**State the contract.** Parts I–III are *how the generators work* (foundations, diffusion, then the challengers). Parts IV–V are *how you actually use them* (conditioning, then the funnel). If a student only retains one half, it should be IV–V — that is where materials genomics differs from a computer-vision course.

**Say what is deliberately excluded.** No molecular generation (different constraints: no lattice, but valence rules), no protein design — we stay with periodic inorganic crystals. Also, no code today; the exercise session runs a pretrained generator through a MACE-MP-0 filter, so the lecture supplies the judgment, the exercise the hands.
